I just found out about PhysLean very recently. Thank you for doing this for humanity! I had similar idea in the past, where I started by formalizing EPR paradox. I wanted to know if this has already been implemented in PhysLean, but there is no search engine for the theorems.

I want to contribute by either formalizing an EPR paradox or implementing a search engine for the theorems.

Oh, nvm, there is already https://www.leanexplore.com/?pkg=PhysLean . I think the link and the link name would have been clearer if it directly links to https://www.leanexplore.com/?pkg=PhysLean instead of just https://www.leanexplore.com/. And call it "Search PhysLean" instead.

There is also: https://leandex.projectnumina.ai which I believe is a newer version of leanexplore.

I think https://www.leanexplore.com/ allows you to search Mathlib and PhysLean simultaneously, whilst https://www.leanexplore.com/?pkg=PhysLean would only restrict you to PhysLean. I think most people would want the former (but I am happy to change this on the PhysLean website if not). I agree using "Search PhysLean" on the website would be better.

We also use to have a version of Loogle for PhysLean but it got too expensive to host.

Concerning EPR paradox - we do not currently have it, and I think it would be a great addition. It would also help us build more in the Quantum Mechanics direction.
I tried and I was able to add both Mathlib and PhysLean as contexts: https://www.leanexplore.com/?pkg=PhysLean&pkg=Mathlib.
https://leandex.projectnumina.ai/?pkg=Mathlib&pkg=PhysLean&use_llm=true is indeed better than leanexplore.com.
Good to know - when I get chance I will update the website
(I've updated the website, including the things discussed here)

Hi everyone, together with @Gabriele Battimelli we just finished Physlib Search. Everything is open source. Here is the repo: https://github.com/Kernel-Science/physlibsearch.git

It's both the UI and the API – Check out the repo for details.

Technical two sentences – We translate each formal Lean 4 declaration into a natural-language name and description using Gemini guided by dependency-ordered context, then embed both the formal and informal representations into a shared vector space using Gemini Embeddings. At query time, a user's plain-English query (optionally expanded via HyDE into a hypothetical Lean declaration) is embedded and matched against the indexed declarations using approximate nearest-neighbor cosine similarity search in ChromaDB.

We intend to maintain this for the community and keep it free and open source!
Do you do PhysLib-specific optimizations, or can the method be reused without modification on Mathlib as well?

Hi all, happy to be around! The core method is largely reusable on Mathlib, in fact, some of it was inspired by LeanSearch, but the informalization prompts are PhysLib-specific and would need to be updated.

Amazing work! The "browse" section in particular seems extremely useful: it gives a natural language view of what's in each file which is much more familiar to physicists, and I can see physlib contributors actually looking at this and think about how to structure a file so that this reads logically. Also, docstrings are definitely lacking in many files and this could serve as a very good guide, or at least inspiration for how to describe the lemmas/theorems.

Some quick suggestions:

  1. currently the #theorem_name on top right of each item only makes it jump to the top of page which doesn't really do anything, is it possible to link to the corresponding https://physlib.io/docs/ page?

  2. is it possible to distinguish between lemma and theorem? as a follow-up, can there be a simple filter to filter defs/lemma/theorems? (seems like a straightforward way to look at a theorem list as discussed here, but also a way to check what are the defs made in each file vs what are the lemmas/theorems being proven without the defs)

  3. (Dark mode please)

Hi all! We just pushed a batch of improvements to PhyslibSearch based on your feedback:

Dark mode — toggle in the header
Submodule navigation — clicking into namespaces on the Browse page now shows child submodules with declaration counts
Docs links — declaration anchors on the Browse page now link to the corresponding physlib.io/docs page
Definition values — expanding a definition now shows the := ... body when present
Clickable breadcrumbs — module paths on search results link directly to the Browse page

Thanks especially to @ZhiKai Pong and @Joseph Tooby-Smith for the detailed suggestions — keep them coming!

Joseph Tooby-Smith said:

I don't know if this is possible, but it would be very nice if it was possible for people to suggest changes through this site e.g. to documentation or even adding new informal or formal results. Maybe out of scope though.

About feedbacks – We put a feedback button in the bottom-right side of each page. So if you leave a feedback in that page we will know it was triggered by something in that page.

About adding new results – we already set things up so that we can simply re-run the crawling and embedding algorithm and it will only add the new results. We're planning to do this every couple of weeks for now, but we can easily find a way to automate it and do daily updates. Especially when Physlib starts growing at a faster pace

Would it also be possible to explain how to decide the architecture for this RAG pipeline :sweat_smile: Like the choice of pipeline is very different from gbrain by
Garry Tan (https://github.com/garrytan/gbrain) and this is right since Lean database is very different in nature (laconic and technical) from a typical tech guy folder. But would be great if you could tell how you arrived at the decisions??

Hey @Shlok Vaibhav — good question, and you're right that gbrain's pipeline would be a poor fit here. The short answer is that the corpus isn't prose, it's formal Lean code, so every non-obvious choice exists to close the distribution gap between "plain-English physics question" and "terse Lean signature." A few of the key calls:

  • Chunking is per-declaration, not per-file or fixed-window. Lean's semantic unit is the declaration, and jixia already exposes name / signature / dependencies that way, so we don't want to slice through that structure.

  • We informalize before embedding. Rather than embedding raw Lean, we first ask Gemini to generate a natural-language name + description for every declaration (Herald-style, arxiv.org/abs/2410.10878). What we actually embed is a concatenation of both the formal signature and the informal description. That way the same vector can be reached by someone who already knows the Lean name and by someone who only has the physics idea in their head. The reason for this embedding was that doing just one of them would alienate half the users.

  • Informalization walks the dependency graph in topological order. When Gemini translates a theorem, it already has the informal descriptions of every symbol that theorem references. We tried that because we wanted to mirror how a mathematician reads a library. Generic RAGs don't have this because prose has no typed dependency graph.

  • On the query side we use HyDE. Gemini rewrites the user's query into a plausible hypothetical Lean declaration and embeds that. Again, putting both sides of the search in the same distribution so nearest-neighbour actually means something.

I did a more complete write-up with file references (with help by Claude :smile:): docs/architecture.md#design-decisions.

Should you have suggestions on how to improve any of that, please let us know. We're open to anything that makes it better

also I still want theorem vs lemma filtering if possible :face_in_clouds:

Hey ZhiKai — thanks a ton for the detailed feedback, this was really valuable! Shipped fixes for all of it:

  • Sidebar getting cut off: the left sidebar is now independently scrollable, so the filter stays reachable even when the library tree is fully expanded. Dual scroll, as you suggested.
  • Filter persistence: the kind filter now sticks as you click around — through the sidebar, breadcrumbs, submodule links, and the root browse page. Also renamed "Clear" → "Reset" per your suggestion.
  • Double := on expand: fixed — turns out the stored value already starts with := in the DB, so we were doubling it.
  • Red LaTeX errors (e.g. on the RealTensor/Vector/Pre/Modules page): tracked this down to the informal-description generator occasionally emitting \mathbb{X} inside \text{...}, which KaTeX (correctly) refuses to parse. Added a client-side sanitizer that rewrites \mathbb{R/C/Z/N/Q/...} to their Unicode equivalents when they appear inside \text{}, so those entries now render properly. Also made truly unparseable LaTeX fall back to plain source text instead of a jarring red error.
  • Bonus: made the browse page properly responsive while I was in there — long names no longer overflow on narrow viewports, and there's a horizontal chip filter on mobile (since the sidebar is hidden there).

On theorem vs lemma filtering: unfortunately in Lean 4, lemma elaborates identically to theorem, so they're stored with the same kind in the DB. Distinguishing them would need a backend change to capture the original surface keyword — happy to look at that next!

Thanks again :folded_hands:

May have already been suggested above, but it would be nice to have the module doc-strings included on the browse pages.

Another suggestion (possibly very hard): Some of the doc-strings are AI generated, so it would be nice if there was an easy way to suggest that a given doc-string (if 'good enough') actually be moved into the Lean file itself. Other features like this would also be great, as it can act a bit like a feedback mechanism to the project itself.
